text: Van Uden collaborated with various local figure painters, and his most original works are his drawings. His father, Artus van Uden, was Antwerp's city painter, a position that required him to paint the city's buildings and to refurbish and gild the statues of the city and the pieces used in the ommegang. His brother Jacob also became a landscape painter. Lucas was a landscape painter, draughtsman and engraver who lived and worked in Antwerp.

Freudenberger studied with Emanuel Handmann from 1761 to 1764 and followed him from Bern to Basel in the final year of his training. After several months in Lausanne on portrait commissions, he left for Paris in 1765 with the engraver Adrian Zingg. After training in Switzerland and working in Paris, he returned to Bern, where rural genre scenes became central to his work. He belonged to the Bernese Kleinmeister tradition.

Alma Mahler, author and composer, was the eldest daughter of the Austrian landscape painter Schindler. His family had run cotton spinning mills in Fischamend, a village south of Vienna, since the 17th century. His father died of lung cancer when Emil was only four, and his mother soon took him to Pressburg. In 1849 she married a second lieutenant, Mathias Eduard Nepalleck.

Meyssens was baptised in Antwerp in 1640 and trained there with his father, the prominent engraver and print publisher Joannes Meyssens. He was registered as a wijnmeester, the son of a master, in the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke in 1660 to 1661. He later moved to Vienna and worked there for the rest of his life. He is known for reproductive prints after famous painters and for portraits.

Farington worked as an English landscape painter and diarist in the 18th century. He was the second of seven sons of the rector of Warrington and vicar of Leigh. Three of his brothers, William, Henry and Richard, were employed in the naval service of the East India Company, and his brother George became a painter like him. His views include Deptford Dockyard.

Pechstein belonged to the Die Brücke group. He came from Zwickau, where his father worked in a textile mill and the family of eight lived on that one salary. An early contact with the art of Vincent van Gogh pushed him toward expressionism. He fought on the Western Front in the First World War, and the Nazis classified his art as degenerate. More than 300 of his paintings were removed from German museums.

Bol had a successful career in Flanders, then left for the Dutch Republic during the Siege of Antwerp. He is known for landscapes, allegorical and biblical scenes and genre paintings in a late Northern Mannerist style. His landscape work had an important influence on the next generation of Dutch landscape painters. His prints, after his own designs and after Flemish masters such as Pieter Brueghel the Elder, helped spread their themes.

Palma Giovane, born Iacopo Negretti, came from a Venetian family of painters and was the great-nephew of Palma Vecchio. After Tintoretto died in 1594, Palma became Venice's dominant artist and perpetuated Tintoretto's style. Outside Venice he received numerous commissions around Bergamo and in Central Europe, most prominently from the connoisseur Emperor Rudolph II in Prague. His Tumbling putti dates from 1611.

The Hague was where Van Uyttenbroeck was born and died. According to the RKD he was the younger brother of the painter Jan Matheus van Wtenbrouck, and he later taught Anthonie van der Croos and perhaps Dirk Dalens the Elder. He painted mostly religious and classical mythological subjects. He was a versatile court painter who also made portraits and Italianate landscapes in the manner of Cornelis van Poelenburch.

Kaiser came from a lithographic business in Graz, which his father Joseph Franz Kaiser owned. He studied at the Vienna Academy beside Josef Danhauser and soon became a serious competitor for the leading Vienna portrait lithographer, Josef Kriehuber. Enthused by the ideas of the revolution, he joined the Academic Legion in 1848 and made portraits during that time. He was a celebrated portrait artist who drew the attention of Empress Elisabeth, and his brother Alexander was an artist too.

Bunchō is best known for his actor prints, yakusha-e, in the narrow hosoban format. He and Katsukawa Shunshō are credited with developing kabuki actor portraiture that aimed at likenesses of the subjects rather than stereotyped faces. Little is known about his life. His birth surname was Mori, and he is believed to have studied painting under Ishikawa Yukimoto of the Kanō school. He was born in Edo in 1726.

The last holder of the post of Premier peintre du Roi, from 1789 to 1791, Vien lost it when the French Revolution abolished the post. He was born in Montpellier. As a protégé of the Comte de Caylus, he entered the studio of Natoire at an early age, and he won the Prix de Rome in 1745. In Rome he applied himself to the study of nature.

Pollard was noted for his mail coach, fox hunting and equine scenes. He was born in Islington, the son of the painter and publisher Robert Pollard. He exhibited at the Royal Academy between 1821 and 1839. He also worked with John Frederick Herring Senior on several horse racing paintings, in which he painted the backgrounds and spectators while Herring painted the horses.

Eilshemius painted mainly landscapes and nudes, but he also wrote musical compositions, verse, novels and short stories, and he published periodicals. He was the son of a Dutch father and a Swiss mother, and his wealthy family lived near Newark, New Jersey. After an education in Europe he spent two years at Cornell University before beginning art studies at the Art Students League of New York. He also studied privately with the landscape painter Robert Crannell Minor and later with Bouguereau.

Malevich is best known as the founder of Suprematism, a radically non-objective form of painting he introduced in 1915. His work and writings pioneered the development of abstract painting in the twentieth century. Born in Kiev to an ethnic Polish family, he worked primarily in Russia and became a leading figure of the Russian avant-garde. He is also placed within the Ukrainian avant-garde. Early in his career he worked in several styles, taking in Impressionism, Symbolism and Fauvism.

Prud'hon was best known in his own time for his allegorical paintings and portraits, and today for his drawings. He painted a portrait of Napoleon's wife, the Empress Josephine. After 1803 he worked so closely with the artist Constance Mayer on many paintings that it is almost impossible to tell where the contribution of one ends and the other begins. He was an early influence on Théodore Géricault. He was born in Cluny.

Van der Heyden was one of the first Dutch painters to specialise in townscapes and became one of the leading architectural painters of the Dutch Golden Age. He painted a number of still lifes at the beginning and the end of his career. He was also an engineer and inventor who made significant contributions to firefighting technology. Together with his brother Nicolaes, a hydraulic engineer, he invented an improvement to firefighting equipment.

An early proponent of skyscrapers, Gilbert designed the Woolworth Building and the United States Supreme Court Building, as well as the state capitols of Minnesota and Arkansas. His public buildings in the Beaux Arts style reflect the optimistic American sense that the nation was heir to Greek democracy and Roman law. His achievements were recognized in his lifetime. He served as president of the American Institute of Architects in 1908.

Born in Switzerland, Morier worked in Britain as a painter of portraits, military subjects and historical scenes. His subjects came from the time of the War of the Austrian Succession and the Jacobite rising of 1745. He specialised in equestrian portraits of kings and nobles. He painted some of the most famous aristocratic figures of his time, including King George II, Frederick, Prince of Wales, and King Frederick V of Denmark.

The son of an instrument maker and inventor in Copenhagen, Marstrand studied at the Metropolitan School but had little interest in books and left around the age of sixteen. He was born in Copenhagen on Christmas Eve and belongs to the Golden Age of Danish painting. He worked as a painter and illustrator. His Svend Estridsen and Bishop Vilhelm dates from 1832.

Griggs was one of the first etchers to be elected to full membership of the Royal Academy. He took part in the final phase of the Etching Revival in Britain and in the late flowering of the Arts and Crafts movement in the Cotswolds, centred in Chipping Campden. Born in Hitchin, Hertfordshire, he worked as an illustrator for the Highways and Byways series of regional guides for the publisher Macmillan. In 1934 he was elected Master of the Art Workers' Guild. He was also an architectural draughtsman and an early conservationist.

Madou studied at the Brussels Academy of Fine Arts as a pupil of Pierre Joseph Célestin François. While he was a draftsman for the topographical military division at Kortrijk, a Brussels publisher gave him a commission for lithographic work. His artistic career began about 1820. Between 1825 and 1827 he contributed to Les Vues pittoresques de la Belgique, to a Life of Napoleon, and to works on the costumes of the Netherlands.

The youngest of nine children of English parents in Lewiston, Maine, Hartley lost his mother when he was eight, and four years later his father remarried Martha Marsden. His birth name was Edmund Hartley, and he took Marsden as his first name in his early twenties. When he was fourteen his sisters moved to Ohio and left him behind. He developed his painting by observing Cubist artists in Paris and Berlin.

The art historian Timothy Clark calls Kyōsai an individualist and an independent, perhaps the last virtuoso in traditional Japanese painting. Kyōsai lived from the Edo period into the Meiji period and saw Japan change from a feudal country into a modern state. The son of a samurai, he was born at Koga. At nine he picked up a human head that had been cut from a corpse in the Kanda river, which was his first shock. He worked briefly as a boy with Utagawa Kuniyoshi and then trained in the Kanō school.

A pupil of Georges Lallemand and Simon Vouet, according to the Netherlands Institute for Art History, Dorigny trained at the Académie de peinture et de sculpture. According to Roger de Piles he married Vouet's daughter. He became the teacher and the father of the painters Nicolas and Louis Dorigny. He was a professor of the Academy when he died in Paris. He worked as a painter and engraver and was born in Saint-Quentin.

Demarteau is one of the people credited with inventing the crayon manner of engraving, and he played an important role in developing that technique. He was one of the key reproductive engravers and publishers of the work of François Boucher. He was born in Liège, and his father was a gunsmith. He worked in Paris for his entire career as an etcher, engraver and publisher.

Kirner was one of seven children of a shoemaker in Furtwangen. For financial reasons he first had to learn art through apprenticeships with a coach painter in Freiburg and a decorative painter in Villingen. His older brother, a portrait painter who had served similar apprenticeships, was admitted to the Augsburg art school in 1822, at the age of twenty-eight. In 1824 Johann was finally able to attend the Academy of Fine Arts. Robbers Attacking Travellers is among his pictures.

Cesio grew up in Rome in the school of Pietro da Cortona, and he was employed on several prominent public works during the pontificate of Alexander VII. He painted historical subjects. In the Quirinal he painted The Judgment of Solomon, and other works of his are in Santa Maria Maggiore and in the Rotunda. He was also an engraver. He was born at Antrodoco, then part of the Papal States, and died at Rieti.

Koester specialised in scenes with ducks. His father was a hosiery manufacturer, and in 1882, following his parents' wishes, he began an apprenticeship at a pharmacy in Winzenheim. After completing his training there, he pursued his own interests and enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts in Karlsruhe, where he studied with Karl Hoff. As a student he supported himself by painting portraits, but he later focused on landscapes. He spent the decade from 1885 to 1895 making study trips.

German-born, Nast became an American caricaturist and editorial cartoonist, often considered the Father of the American Cartoon. He was deeply involved in the political issues of the day, often as a member of the Republican party. He promoted the platform of the Radical Republicans against President Andrew Johnson and supported Republican presidential candidates Ulysses Grant, Rutherford Hayes and Benjamin Harrison. Even so, he repeatedly criticized the 1884 nominee James Blaine.

Zatzka signed many of his works with pseudonyms, among them Joseph Bernard, Bernard Zatzka and Zabateri. He did it to avoid penalties for breaking contracts that limited the amount of artwork he could sell. As a result, some art databases mix up his work under the name Joseph Bernard with that of a French sculptor of the same name. He was an Austrian academic and fantasy painter, born in Vienna in 1859.

Waumans is recorded as an apprentice of Paulus Pontius in the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke in the early 1630s, and as a master in the later 1630s. No documents mention him after 30 May 1661, when he signed the guild's new statutes. He may still have been alive in the 1670s, and some sources suggest he lived longer. He produced engravings after religious paintings by Rubens.

Købke was one of eleven children and grew up at Kastellet, a military fortification in Copenhagen, where his father was head baker. At eleven he had a bout of rheumatic fever, and he made many drawings while he recovered and decided that he would become an artist. At twelve he started his studies at the Royal Academy. He is one of the best-known artists of the Golden Age of Danish painting.

Born Hubert-François Bourguignon in Paris, Gravelot worked as an engraver, book illustrator, designer and drawing-master. He emigrated to London in 1732, where he quickly became a central figure in the introduction of the Rococo style in British design. It spread from London through book illustrations and engraved designs, and through luxury goods in the French taste. His Design for Frame Surrounding the Portrait of Sir Francis Walsingham is among his drawings.

The illegitimate son of a factory owner and his Czech housemaid, Romako was born in Atzgersdorf near Vienna. He studied painting at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, but his teacher, Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller, considered him talentless. Later he studied in Munich under Wilhelm Kaulbach, and then in Venice, Rome and London. His brother Josef von Romako became a naval architect-inspector in the Austro-Hungarian Navy. Nibbling Girl is among his pictures.

Gaspard-Félix Tournachon worked under the pseudonym Nadar as a photographer, caricaturist, journalist, novelist and balloonist. In 1858 he became the first person to take aerial photographs. He was a proponent of heavier-than-air flight. He was born in Paris in 1820, though some sources say Lyon, and his father, Victor Tournachon, was a printer. Many great national collections hold his photographic portraits. His son Paul continued the studio after his death.

Rossetti founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in 1848 with William Holman Hunt and John Everett Millais. He inspired many contemporary artists and writers, such as Swinburne and William Morris. His later work influenced the European Symbolists and was a major precursor of the Aesthetic movement. His art was sensual and medievalist. He worked as a poet, illustrator, painter and translator. His drawings include a portrait of Elizabeth Siddal resting with a parasol.

Rome was Gérard's birthplace, where his father had a post in the house of the French ambassador, and his mother was Italian. A student of Jacques-Louis David, he became one of the leading painters of the First French Empire and the Bourbon Restoration. He was court painter to Napoleon and later First Painter to Louis XVIII and Charles X. He was titled Baron in 1809 and nicknamed the painter of kings, the king of painters.

Jelgerhuis made his fame mainly as a travelling portrait painter, and he has no fewer than 7,763 portraits to his credit. He was born in Leeuwarden and died in Amsterdam. He taught his son, Johannes Jelgerhuis, who became an accomplished painter, illustrator and actor. He also worked as an engraver and draftsman. His Begijnensteeg with the entrance to the Begijnhof dates from 1744.

Brébiette lived and worked in Italy, much of the time in Rome, from 1617 to about 1625. He and his wife had seven children. Many of his etchings and some of his drawings survive, but only one of his signed paintings has been positively identified and widely accepted as his, The Rape of Proserpina by Pluto, an oil on canvas now in the Musée des Beaux-Arts et d'Archéologie in Châlons-en-Champagne. He was born in Mantes-sur-Seine.

Born Chaim-Iche Solomonovich Sutin in Smilavichy, Soutine became a French painter of the School of Paris. He made a major contribution to the Expressionist movement while living and working in Paris. He was inspired by classic painting in the European tradition, such as Rembrandt and Courbet. His individual style cared more about shape, color and texture than representation, and it served as a bridge to Abstract Expressionism.

Maillol decided at an early age to become a painter, and in 1881 he moved from Banyuls-sur-Mer to Paris to study art. He began his career as a painter and developed an early interest in the decorative arts. From his early forties he became primarily interested in sculpture. His work inspired artists such as Picasso and Henry Moore. He was a French Catalan sculptor, painter and printmaker.

Hopfer is widely believed to have been the first to use etching in printmaking, at the end of the 15th century. He also worked in woodcut. Art historians ignored his etchings for years, but more recent scholarship credits him with establishing the salability of etchings and with introducing the print publisher business model. Unlike most later prints, which were etched on copper plates, his etchings were made on iron plates, the material he was used to working with in steel plate armour.

Ślewiński's mother died in childbirth, and he grew up in a landowning family in Nowy Białynin. His cousin, the painter Józef Chełmoński, noticed his artistic talent and advised his father to enroll him at the drawing school run by Wojciech Gerson. His father resisted at first, but finally agreed. In 1886 he inherited the family properties in Pilaszkowice Pierwsze, which soon led to his financial ruin. He was one of Gauguin's students and a leading artist of the Young Poland movement.

Moll studied art at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, where his teachers were Christian Griepenkerl and Emil Jakob Schindler, the father of Alma Mahler-Werfel. He was one of the artists of the Vienna Secession who took inspiration from the pointillist techniques of the French Impressionists. He painted as an Art Nouveau artist in Vienna at the start of the twentieth century. He was an early supporter of the Nazis. Hohe Warte is among his pictures.

In his lifetime Oswald Achenbach was counted among the most important landscape painters of Europe, and through his teaching he influenced the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf. His brother Andreas, who was twelve years older, was also among the most important German landscape painters of the 19th century. The two brothers were humorously called the A and O of Landscapes, a play on their initials. Oswald painted Italian scenes such as On the Beach at Naples.

The son of a tailor, Dagnan was raised by his grandfather after his father emigrated to Brazil, and he later added his grandfather's name, Bouveret, to his own. From 1869 he studied at the École des Beaux-Arts under Alexandre Cabanel and Jean-Léon Gérôme. He exhibited at the Salon from 1875 and won the first-class medal there in 1880. He became one of the leading artists of the French naturalist school and painted several paintings depicting Brittany.

Breenbergh painted Italian and Italianate landscapes, first in Rome and later in Amsterdam. Little is known of his early life. In his Schouburg, Arnold Houbraken mentioned him and asked readers to write to him with more news of Breenbergh's biography. Houbraken had been told that Breenbergh was born in Utrecht and had been a master of Cornelis van Poelenburch, which he knew to be impossible.

A goldsmith's son from Caen, Lasne belonged to the Guild of Saint Luke in Antwerp in 1617 and probably worked under the direction of Rubens and Van Dyck. At that time he engraved Rubens's now-lost Susanna and the Elders, which carries a dedication from Rubens to the Dutch humanist Anna Roemers Visscher. He was in Paris by 1621, and in 1633 he became the official engraver for King Louis XIII. In France he engraved a number of portraits.

Egner took her first drawing lessons in Graz with Hermann von Königsbrunn and then went to Düsseldorf, where she studied with Carl Jungheim. In 1882 she went to live with her mother in Vienna, but she spent her summers at the art colony in Plankenberg Castle near Neulengbach, taking lessons from Emil Jakob Schindler until 1887. A study trip to England followed. Shortly after, her first exhibition was held at the Vienna Künstlerhaus.

Born in Snitterfield, Warwickshire, near Stratford-upon-Avon, Wootton is best remembered as a pioneer in the painting of sporting subjects, together with Peter Tillemans and James Seymour. In his day he was considered the finest practitioner of the genre. His paintings were fashionable and were sought after by the highest ranks of British society, including George II, Frederick, Prince of Wales, and the Duke of Marlborough. He also painted battle scenes and landscapes.

Rembrandt Peale was named by his father, the artist Charles Willson Peale, after the 17th-century Dutch painter. He was the third of six surviving children, because eleven others had died. He was a prolific portrait painter, especially acclaimed for his likenesses of George Washington and Thomas Jefferson. After a stay in Paris in his early thirties, French neoclassicism influenced his style. He also worked as a museum keeper.

Huet came from a family of artists. His uncle Christophe and his father Nicolas were both painters. He apprenticed with the animal painter Charles Dagomer, and about 1764 he entered the studio of Jean-Baptiste Le Prince. His Dog Attacking Geese, now in the Louvre, was well received at the Salon in 1769. Later he designed scenic vignettes printed on cotton at the toiles de Jouy factory of Oberkampf. His attempts at the grand manner of history painting were not approved.

Torres-García spent most of his adult life in Spain. Later he travelled and lived in the United States, Italy, France and Uruguay. He founded influential schools and groups, among them the Escola de Decoració in Barcelona. In Paris he co-founded Cercle et Carré, the first European abstract-art group, which brought together artists such as Piet Mondrian and Wassily Kandinsky. He worked as a painter and theorist, and also as a teacher and author.

Testa, the son of a dealer in secondhand goods in Lucca, was in Rome by the late 1620s, where he was known as il Lucchesino. Joachim von Sandrart said he found Testa drawing among the ancient ruins and set him to making preparatory drawings for the Giustiniani engravings. By 1630 he worked in the studio of Domenichino. He also filled five large volumes with drawings of antiquities for Cassiano dal Pozzo's Paper Museum. His public paintings were largely unsuccessful, but his prints and drawings carried his reputation.

Wandelaar trained under Jacob Folkema, Gilliam van der Gouwen and Gerard de Lairesse. He made a name in anatomical art after drawing for Frederik Ruysch. Pieter Lyonet and Abraham Delfos studied with him. For Bernhard Siegfried Albinus he illustrated and engraved the plates of the Tabulae sceleti et musculorum corporis humani, and the second London edition of 1749 shows a human skeleton with the rhinoceros Clara added in the background. He died in Leiden.

Growing up on a farm on Staten Island as the oldest of eight children, Cropsey taught himself to draw while absent from school through poor health. He trained as an architect under Joseph Trench and learned watercolor from Edward Maury. In 1843 he opened an architecture office. Within a year he was exhibiting watercolors at the National Academy of Design, and he soon turned entirely to landscape painting. He traveled in England, France, Switzerland and Italy from 1847. Hudson River School landscapes are what he is best known for.

Holsteyn, son of the glass painter Pieter Holsteyn I and brother of the painter Cornelis, worked in Haarlem, Amsterdam, Munster and Enkhuizen. Houbraken, who called him Holstein, quoted Samuel Ampzing on him as a good glass painter. His pupil was the painter Josua Breckerveld. He signed with the monogram PH. Insects and birds appeared in watercolors painted in his style that were sold at an auction in Haarlem in 1706, and Herman Henstenburgh was influenced by them.

A baker's son from Berlin, Gramatté enlisted at the beginning of the First World War, though poor health often exempted him from combat duty. He studied mostly at the Kunstgewerbeschule in Berlin and opened his own studio in 1917. After marrying the Russian pianist Sonia Fridman in 1920 he joined the circle of Die Brücke. He travelled through France, Italy and Spain. Hospital stays and long periods at the spa on Hiddensee marked his last years, and he died of intestinal tuberculosis. Karl Schmidt-Rottluff designed his grave monument.

Luks began his working life in vaudeville, playing the Pennsylvania and New Jersey circuit with his younger brother. His father was a physician and apothecary. His mother was an amateur painter and musician. He studied briefly at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts before he traveled to Europe. Back home he worked as a newspaper illustrator and cartoonist in Philadelphia, where he joined the group around Robert Henri that set out to defy the values of the National Academy of Design. His best-known paintings show the poor of Manhattan's Lower East Side.

Chaplin came from Les Andelys, the son of a French mother and an English father who traded in art. He studied at the École des Beaux-Arts from 1840 and took private lessons in the studio of Michel Martin Drolling. In 1845 he entered the Paris Salon with a Portrait of the Artist's Mother. His techniques included pastel and lithography. Mary Cassatt, Louise Abbéma and Louise Jopling studied in the classes he gave for women at his studio. He died in Paris and lies in Père Lachaise.

Grimm, born in Burgdorf, first aspired to be a poet and published a volume of poems in 1762. He then moved to Bern. There he studied under Johann Ludwig Aberli, a specialist in topographical views of the Swiss Alps, and supplied drawings for Friedrich von Hagedorn's Poetische Werke. At 32 he went to Paris to study under Johann Georg Wille. Later he illustrated books such as Gilbert White's The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne. Until 1764 he worked in oils.

Downman set off for Italy in 1773 with Joseph Wright of Derby, a pregnant Ann Wright and Richard Hurleston. Their ship sheltered three weeks in Nice before it reached Livorno in February 1774. He was the son of an attorney from St Neots and was baptised at Eynesbury, not born near Ruabon as earlier works assumed. After early schooling in Ruabon and briefly in Liverpool, he attended the Royal Academy schools and spent a while in the studio of Benjamin West. He later settled in Cambridge, then in London, where he contributed to various exhibitions.

A student of Katsukawa Shunshō, possibly the master's first, Shunkō lived in Nihonbashi Hasegawachō in Edo. His earliest known work is the set of illustrations to Talks about Debut Plays, from 1766. From about 1771 he designed actor prints, which he signed with a small jar-shaped seal beside the larger one of his master. That seal gave him the nickname Kotsubo, meaning small jar. He is generally credited with designing the first large-head actor portraits. At 45 he became partially paralyzed and stopped designing prints, but he kept painting with his left hand.

Thesleff grew up in Helsinki as the eldest daughter of five siblings, and her father painted as an amateur. After private lessons she studied for two years at the Finnish Art Society Drawing School under Gunnar Berndtson. In 1891 she moved to Paris and enrolled at the Académie Colarossi. She never married and kept a family estate at Murole in Ruovesi. At the start of her career she painted symbolist works in a style close to Eugène Carrière, though she insisted that Édouard Manet had influenced her most. Later she moved toward expressionism, most notably in landscapes.

Rousselet, born in Paris, was the son of a bookseller who was possibly also a printmaker. It is unknown with whom he studied engraving, but his work was inspired by Abraham Bloemaert. He married Judith Le Goux in 1645, and they had fourteen children. One of them was the sculptor Jean Rousselet. Much of his engraving reproduced works by other artists, among them Claude Vignon, Jacques Stella, Nicolas Poussin and his friend Charles Le Brun. Unlike Jacques Callot or Claude Mellan, he created few original designs of his own.

Nicknamed the French Borromini, Oppenord was one of the initiators of the Rocaille and Rococo styles. His father Alexandre-Jean Oppenord was an ébéniste from Guelders who became ébéniste du Roi in 1684, with lodgings in the Galeries du Louvre. As a boy the son trained in the studio of Jules Hardouin-Mansart. In 1692 he went to Rome as a royal pensioner for eight years. There he largely ignored the remains of Classical Antiquity and sketched the Baroque sculptural ornaments of the preceding generations instead. He worked as a designer for the Bâtiments du Roi.

Kallmorgen, the son of an architect from Hamburg, took his first drawing lessons from his uncle. In 1875 he enrolled at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf. There he studied with Andreas Müller and Ernst Deger. He then moved to the Academy of Fine Arts in Karlsruhe and finished his studies under Gustav Schönleber. Together with Schönleber and Hermann Baisch he traveled to France, Belgium and Holland, and on his return he married the flower painter Margarethe Hormuth. In 1889 he became a founder of the Grötzingen artists' colony.

Barocci, whose original name was Federico Fiori, was nicknamed Il Baroccio. He was apprenticed first with his father Ambrogio, a sculptor of local eminence, and then with the painter Battista Franco Veneziano in Urbino. In 1548 he went with his uncle Bartolommeo Genga to Rome, where he worked in the studio of Taddeo and Federico Zuccari. After four years he returned to Urbino. Pope Pius IV then invited him back to help decorate the Vatican Belvedere Palace, where he fell ill with intestinal complaints.

Baptized in Brussels as the son of a linen merchant, Sweerts left little record of his early life and none of his training. He arrived in Rome in 1646 and stayed active there for several years. In Rome he joined the circle of Flemish and Dutch painters around Pieter van Laer, known as the Bamboccianti. His work in that genre shows greater stylistic mastery and social sensitivity than that of the others. He led an itinerant life and worked in Brussels, Amsterdam, Persia and Goa. Successful in his lifetime, he fell into obscurity until the 20th century.

Halonen grew up on a farm in Lapinlahti, where his father also worked as a decorative painter for churches in neighbouring districts. He often went along on those painting trips and so learned the craft. After four years at the Art Society's Drawing School in Helsinki he won a scholarship to study abroad. In 1890 he went to Paris, studying first at the Academie Julian and later under Paul Gauguin. A trip in 1896 took him through Florence, Siena, Rome and Naples to study early Renaissance art. He married a music student, and they had eight children.
